title: How to Practice Lament
excerpt: Lament is the prayer the modern church forgot. It is not unbelief and it is not whining. It is the language faith speaks when the world is broken and God seems silent.
body:
A third of the Psalms are laments, and most of us have never been taught to pray one. We were given praise and thanksgiving and petition, the prayers for when things are mostly fine, and then when things were not fine we discovered we had no vocabulary at all. So we went silent, or we faked the praise, or we left. The church handed us a prayer language for half of life and acted surprised when we had nothing to say in the other half. Lament is the missing half. It is how the people of God have always prayed in the dark, and it is time we learned it again.

## Know what lament actually is

Lament is honest complaint addressed to God in the confidence that he is listening. That definition has three loads in it. It is honest, so it does not pretend. It is addressed to God, so it is not mere venting into the void. And it is built on confidence, so even at its most furious it is an act of faith, because you do not pour out your anguish to someone you believe is absent. Lament is not the opposite of trust. It is trust under the conditions of suffering.

## Follow the shape the Psalms give you

Most laments move through a pattern, and learning it gives you a path when you cannot find one. First, you turn to God by name. Second, you bring the complaint, the actual raw grievance, what is wrong and how much it hurts. Third, you ask, boldly, for what you want him to do. Fourth, most laments turn, somewhere, toward trust, not because the problem is solved but because the relationship holds. Psalm 13 does all of this in six verses. You do not have to manufacture the turn. Sometimes it comes. Sometimes, as in Psalm 88, it never does, and that prayer is in the Bible too.

## Say the complaint without softening it

This is the part we flinch from. We were trained to be polite with God, to wrap every grievance in a qualifier. Lament refuses the wrapping. "You have laid me in the depths of the pit." "Why do you hide your face?" "My tears have been my food day and night." These are not the prayers of weak faith. They are in Scripture, preserved by the Spirit, prayed by the most faithful people in the book. Stop protecting God from your honesty. He can hear the real thing, and the real thing is the only thing he can heal.

## Make it concrete, not abstract

Do not lament "the brokenness of the world" in general. Lament the specific thing. The empty side of the bed. The test results. The friend who betrayed you. The prayer you have prayed a thousand times that heaven has not answered. Lament is particular or it is performance. Name the actual wound, the actual person, the actual day it happened.

## Let it be communal, not only private

Lament was never meant to be only a solitary cry. Israel lamented together. The book of Lamentations is a city weeping over its own ruins. When you sit with someone in their suffering, you can lament with them, give voice to the grievance they are too exhausted to speak. And when you lead or gather others, make room for the prayer that does not resolve, so that the suffering among you do not have to fake a joy they do not feel just to belong.

**This week:** Write your own lament. Four short movements. Address God by name. Tell him exactly what is wrong, with no softening. Ask him for what you actually want. Then, only if it is true, write one line of trust, and if it is not true yet, leave it blank and let the blank be honest. Pray it three times this week.

The world is broken, and it is right to say so, out loud, to the One who made it and has not yet finished mending it. Lament is the prayer that refuses to lie about the wound and refuses to stop talking to God about it. It does not resolve the suffering. It does something harder and better. It keeps you in the conversation until the morning comes.
